section.title: OutputVal and OutputValue Classes
section.para: OutputVal and its derived classes describe the quantities computed by Outputs. OutputValue and its subclasses handle reference counting for OutputVals.

listitem.simpara: SRC/engine/outputval.spy: Python code included in the SWIG output

refsection.title: Description
refsection.para: The OutputVal classes are used to ferry values from the finite element mesh out to the Python output machinery. The classes give the output machinery the ability to decide what further processing is possible (e.g, computing components or invariants). The OutputVal subclasses are wrappers for the actual datatypes (floats, tensors, etc). The OutputValue class provides a generic reference-counted wrapper for all of the OutputVal subclasses.

The concrete OutputVal subclasses are split into two varieties according to two intermediate classes:
ArithmeticOutputVal subclasses describe outputs that can be manipulated numerically and statistically, such as the components of &Fields; and &Fluxes;, or values that can be computed from them.
NonArithmeticOutputVal subclasses describe all outputs that don't fit in other class. This includes things like the values of an modulus, or components of color. It is technically possible to perform arithmetic with those quantities, but not meaningful.
There are three subclasses of ArithmeticOutputVal:
ScalarOutputVal for scalar quantities.
VectorOutputVal for vector quantities.
SymmMatrix3 for symmetric 3×3 tensor quantities.

refsection.title: Assignment operator
refsection.programlisting: virtual const OutputVal& operator=(const OutputVal& other);
refsection.para: The assignment operator copies the value of other to the current object. It is an error if the concrete derived class of other not the same as the class of this.

The methods defined in the subclasses have a covariant return type, returning a reference to the subclass, not to &OutputVal;. The concrete subclasses also define a non-virtual assigment operator that takes a subclass instance argument.

refsection.title: Values
refsection.para: value_list returns a flat list of the components of the OutputVal, as floating point numbers. For SymmMatrix3 objects, value_list returns the six independent components in Voigt order.
When used in C++, value_list returns a pointer to a vector that must be explicitly deallocated.

refsection.title: Index
refsection.para: getIndex converts the standard string representation of the name of a component to an IndexP object, which can be used to access components. The form of the string depends on the OutputVal subclass.

TODO: Move this paragraph to subclasses. For SymmMatrix3 objects, the argument str must be a two character string made up of only 'x', 'y', and 'z'. For VectorOutputVals, str must be exactly "x", "y", or "z". For ScalarOutputVals, str is ignored.

refsection.title: Components
refsection.para: components returns an Components object suitable for iterating over the components of the OutputVal. See for more information about iterating over components.

refsection.title: Dimension
refsection.para: dim returns the number of components in the OutputVal. It's 1 for scalars, something for vectors, and 6 for symmetric 3×3 tensors.

refsection.title: Clone
refsection.para: Create a copy of the OutputVal. In C++ it is the caller's responsibility to delete the copy, if the reference counting wrapper is not used.

refsection.title: Description
refsection.para: ArithmeticOutputVal is an abstract class derived from OutputVal. It is used as a base class for numerical Outputs on which arithmetic can be performed.

refsection.title: Direct component access
refsection.programlisting: double operator[](const FieldIndex& index) const; double& operator[](const FieldIndex& index);
refsection.para: operator[] (in C++) and __getitem__ (in Python) retrieve a component of the data wrapped by the OutputVal. The argument must be a FieldIndex of the appropriate type, or (in C++) a generic IndexP wrapper for it.

refsection.title: Arithmetic operators
refsection.para: Arithmetic operations on ArithmeticOutputVals are allowed where they make sense, both in C++ and Python. In particular, it's possible to add or subtract two ArithmeticOutputVals of the same type, and it's possible to multiply or divide an ArithmeticOutputVal by a floating point number.

Note that in many cases it's not necessary or desirable to do arithmetic with ArithmeticOutputVal objects. The point of ArithmeticOutputVals is to provide a generic wrapper (via virtual functions in the base class) to different kinds of output data. In any non-generic situation, in which the type of the data is known, it's better to do the arithmetic on the underlying data directly, and then create a new ArithmeticOutputVal (of the appropriate flavor) to hold the result.

refsection.title: Component by component operations
refsection.para: These functions operate on the components of an OutputVal. They operate in-place. That is, obj.component_square() changes obj itself. It doesn't return a new object.

refsection.title: Magnitude
refsection.para: magnitude() returns the magnitude of the ArithmeticOutputVal.

refsection.title: Zero
refsection.para: zero() returns a new instance of the ArithmeticOutputVal subclass with all of its components set to 0. In C++ it is the caller's responsibility to delete the copy, if the reference counting wrapper &ArithmeticOutputValue; is not used.
zero is used to initiate integrals and other recursive numerical operations.

refsection.title: One
refsection.para: one() returns a new instance of the ArithmeticOutputVal subclass with all of its components set to 1. In C++ it is the caller's responsibility to delete the copy, if the reference counting wrapper &ArithmeticOutputValue; is not used.
one is used in some integrals and statistical analyses.

refsynopsisdiv.para: These synopses only list methods that are not described in the base classes, or need additional explanation here. See &OutputVal; and &ArithmeticOutputVal; for the base class methods.

refsection.title: Description
refsection.para: ScalarOutputVal is a concrete subclass of &OutputVal; and &ArithmeticOutputVal;. It is used by Outputs that compute scalar quantities. Each ScalarOutputVal wreps a single floating point number in a way that allows generic output methods to operate on it.

refsection.title: Constructors
refsection.para: In Python, ScalarOutputVals are constructed from a single floating point number, its initial value. In addition, in C++ the constructor with no arguments is equvialent to ScalarOutputVal(0.0), and the copy constructor copies the value from another ScalarOutputVal.

refsection.title: Assignment
refsection.programlisting: const ScalarOutputVal& operator=(const ScalarOutputVal& other); const ScalarOutputVal& operator=(const OutputVal& other);
refsection.para: The first form shown above, with a ScalarOutputVal argument, is a non-virtual method. The second is the concrete implementation of the virtual assignment operator declared in the &OutputVal; base class. Both do what you would expect, copying the value from other to *this.

refsection.title: getIndex
refsection.para: Generically, getIndex converts the customary string representation of an index into a &FieldIndex;. For a ScalarOutputVal, the only &FieldIndex; is so getIndex return that and ignores its argument. The argument still needs to be provided, though, and needs to a std::string in C++ or a string in Python.

refsection.title: Value
refsection.para: Return the value wrapped by the ScalarOutputVal. value() is equivalent to the generic function OutputVal::operator[](IndexP&), but more efficient.

In C++, a new value can be assigned to an existing ScalarOutputVal like this:
ScalarOutputVal v; v.value() = 3; In Python, the assignment operator can be used:
v = ScalarOutputVal(3) but beware that this doesn't change the value of whatever c referred to before the assignment.

refsection.title: Less than
refsection.para: The less-than operator for ScalarOutputVals compares their values.

refsection.title: Arithmetic operators
refsection.para: In C++ the arithmetic operators defined in &ArithmeticOutputVal; are augmented with the binary operators listed above. They all do what you would expect.

In Python, the binary operators are defined in the base class, with the exception of __rtruediv__. It's defined here so that
x = ScalarOutputVal(2.) y = 1/x is legal. __rtruediv__ is not defined for any other subclasses of &ArithmeticOutputVal;.

refsection.title: Description
refsection.para: VectorOutputVal is a concrete subclass of &OutputVal; and &ArithmeticOutputVal; that is used by Outputs; that compute floating-point vector quantities. The size of the vector is variable. Each VectorOutputVal wraps a single vector in a way that allows generic output methods to operate on it.

refsection.title: Methods
refsection.para: Methods that VectorOutputVal has in common with other OutputVals are discussed in &OutputVal; and &ArithmeticOutputVal;.

refsection.title: Constructor
refsection.para: The integer argument to the VectorOutputVal constructor specifies the number of components of the vector. The components are initialized to zero.

refsection.title: Size
refsection.para: size() returns the length (number of components) of the vector.

refsection.title: Magnitude
refsection.para: magnitude returns the length (L2 norm) of the vector.

refsection.title: Direct component access
refsection.programlisting: double operator[](int i) const; double& operator[](int i);
refsection.para: VectorOutputVal::operator[](int) is a shortcut for the generic function OutputVal::operator[](IndexP&).

refsection.title: SymmMatrix3 Methods
refsection.para: Methods that SymmMatrix3 has in common with other OutputVals are discussed in and .

refsection.title: Constructors
refsection.programlisting: SymmMatrix3(); SymmMatrix3(double xx, double yy, double zz, double yz, double xz, double xy);
def __init__(self, xx, yy, zz, yz, xz, xy)
refsection.para: In C++, there are two constructors for the SymmMatrix3 class. The version with no arguments creates a SymmMatrix3 with all components set to zero. In the second version, all of the components are specified by the arguments, in Voigt order.

In Python, all of the arguments to the SymmMatrix3 constructor are optional, with the missing ones defaulting to zero. It's best to use keyword arguments, like this:
tensor = SymmMatrix3(xy=1.23, xz=4.56) If keywords aren't used, then the arguments must be in Voigt order.

refsection.title: Direct component access
refsection.programlisting: double operator[](const SymTensorIndex&) const; double& operator[](const SymTensorIndex&);
refsection.para: SymmMatrix3::operator[](const SymTensorIndex&) is a shortcut for the generic function OutputVal::operator[](IndexP&).
In Python, the ij argument is a SymTensorIndex.

refsection.title: Trace
refsection.para: trace returns the sum of the diagonal entries of the SymmMatrix3 object.

refsection.title: Determinant
refsection.para: determinant returns the determinant of the SymmMatrix3 object.

refsection.title: Second invariant
refsection.para:
The secondInvariant of a SymmMatrix3 \(\sigma\) is
\[ \sigma_{xx}\sigma_{zz} + \sigma_{xx}\sigma_{yy} + \sigma_{yy}\sigma_{zz} - \sigma_{xy}^2 - \sigma_{xz}^2 - \sigma_{yz}^2 \]

refsection.title: Eigenvalues
refsection.para: These functions return the eigenvalues of the SymmMatrix3 object. It's guaranteed that minEigenvalue() <= midEigenvalue() <= maxEigenvalue().

refsect2.title: C++ Synopsis

refsection.title: Description
refsection.para: The OutputValue class is a reference counting wrapper for the various OutputVal classes. That means that an OutputValue contains a pointer to an OutputVal, and takes care of deleting the OutputVal when no more OutputValues are using it.
OutputValues should not be created explicitly, except by functions like Field::output. They should never be created in Python at all, since that confuses the reference counting.

valueRef returns a reference to the OutputVal wrapped inside the OutputValue. This call does not increment the reference count of the OutputVal, so the programmer must ensure that the returned OutputVal reference does not outlive the OutputValue object.
valuePtr is just like valueRef, except that it returns a pointer instead of a reference. This can be more convenient in some situations.

valueClone is like valuePtr and valueRef, except that it returns a pointer to a new copy of the underlying OutputVal. It is the programmers responsibility to ensure that the pointer is eventually deallocated. valueClone should be use in situations in which the OutputValue might be deallocated before the program is finished with the OutputVal.

The majority of the arithmetic operators available for OutputVals are also available for OutputValues, but only in C++. (The restriction to C++ is because OutputValues are converted to OutputVals by swig typemaps when being passed from C++ to Python, at least in all of the cases in which they're used in Outputs.)
The C++ operator[] and the Python __getitem__ return a component of the OutputValue's underlying OutputVal, given an IndexP of the right variety.
